short.lead: The grilling session for #306 (house-rules: restructure into a shared core with project boundaries and six optional sub-plugins) is done. This page gathers every answer from the five rounds into ten topics. Each topic lists what it creates or changes, one line per decision, and a "Decided by" box names each answer: the round, what the question asked, and what you chose. You confirmed this summary on 2026-10-19.
short.hint: Tap a topic to see what it creates or changes and which answers decided it.
items: stop
Safety
Deletes and risky git commands
done
Deleting a file git can restore is allowed on the agent's own branch.
On anyone else's branch the delete is refused, and the refusal says why.
Risky git commands are refused with the safe way named; you are asked only when no safe way exists.
A branch is the agent's own when its name starts with the agent prefix or an extra prefix from the settings.
A snapshot branch is deleted once its helper's work is merged.
Round 1, question 1, deleting a committed, unchanged file: allowed on the agent's own branch, refused on anyone else's (your own answer).
Round 1, question 2, force-push, branch deletes and commits on a branch that isn't the agent's: refused with the safe way named.
Round 2, question 5, what makes a branch the agent's own: its name starts with the agent prefix or an extra prefix in the settings.
Round 2, question 7, who clears snapshot branches: each is deleted once its helper's work is merged.
Deletes and risky commands are asked about or refused case by case
One rule: the agent's own branch is free, anyone else's is protected
You are asked only when no safe way exists
check
Evidence
Tests and checks
done
Test suites run twice, helpers included.
The agent never skips a check on its own; a slow, paid or unreachable check is named and you are asked.
Skipping a test or hiding a failure is only ever your decision.
Unity batch mode checks a compile only when no Unity command-line tool or editor plugin can.
Round 1, question 3, how many times a suite runs before a success claim: twice, everywhere.
Round 2, question 12, when a check may be skipped for cost: never by the agent; over 10 minutes, paid or unreachable means it asks you (your own answer).
Round 1, question 15, when to use Unity batch mode: only when no Unity command-line tool or editor plugin can check the compile.
hammer
Helpers
How helper agents work
done
A helper with a question only you can answer stops and reports it to the parent session.
A helper's report quotes the real RESULT line and every failure line.
Worktree autosave credits its commits like every other commit and pushes without force to a new snapshot branch.
The sweep commits a finished helper's leftovers only inside its own worktree.
Round 1, question 4, a helper with a question only you can answer: it stops and the parent session asks you.
Round 1, question 5, how much a helper's report quotes: the real RESULT line and every failure line, no limit.
Round 1, question 12, how autosave commits and pushes: the same credit rule as every commit, no force-push, a fresh snapshot branch each time.
Round 1, question 13, whether the sweep may commit a helper's leftovers: yes, only in that helper's own worktree.
list
Scope
Issues, features and stages
done
An obvious bug outside the request becomes an issue, named in the reply.
Every feature that reaches a build plan gets GitHub issues.
A feature that is one step of a bigger one passes QA on its own; the parent closes with its last child.
The parent is found through GitHub's sub-issue link.
An approval counts before its decisions-log entry exists; the entry is needed before the next stage.
Stage moves on pull requests and labels are written rules; an edit attempt never moves a stage.
Round 1, question 6, an obvious bug in a file being edited: not fixed unasked; it becomes an issue.
Round 1, question 8, when a feature needs GitHub issues: whenever it reaches a build plan.
Round 1, question 9, whether a step of a bigger feature can pass QA on its own: yes.
Round 2, question 8, how a feature knows its parent: GitHub's sub-issue link.
Round 1, question 10, an approval that arrives before its log entry: accepted; the entry is required before the next stage.
Round 1, question 11, the design loop's automatic stage moves: kept as written rules, and an edit attempt never moves a stage.
eye
Pages
Where pages are built and how you read them
done
Local sessions build every page on your machine and publish to claude.ai only when you ask.
Cloud sessions publish every page privately to claude.ai and link it, because tapping an HTML file there shows raw code.
The page file is always written under docs/plans/ and committed.
Round 1, question 7, where pages are built: locally for every plan and long reply, published only when asked.
Round 5, question 1, how a cloud session makes a page readable: publish it privately to claude.ai and link that.
Pages are local files only
Local files, plus a private claude.ai link in cloud sessions
A page opens with one tap on your phone
hand
Identity
The agent's name, credit and branches
done
Identity and taste become settings; safety and evidence rules stay fixed.
"Claude" is never the default credit, and your name never goes on someone else's work.
The agent's name is your GitHub login, lowercased, plus "sAgent": ajw2003sAgent.
It is the commit author's name, with your own email.
Credit lines read "Committed by ajw2003sAgent" and "Opened by ajw2003sAgent".
Branches are named ajw2003sAgent/<topic>; AjsAgent/ and claude/ stay as extra agent prefixes, and nothing is renamed.
Round 1, question 16, which rules become settings: identity and taste, never Claude as credit (your own answer).
Round 2, question 1, where the agent's name comes from: the GitHub login plus sAgent.
Round 2, question 2, where the name appears on a commit: as the author's name, with your email.
Round 2, question 3, what the credit line says: Committed by, or Opened by, ajw2003sAgent.
Round 2, question 4, the branch prefix: the agent name.
Round 2, question 6, the 21 AjsAgent/ and 60 claude/ branches: both prefixes stay as extra agent prefixes.
"AjsAgent" and "AJ's agent" are written into the code
The name, credit line and prefix come from settings
Anyone can install the plugin under their own name
lock
Settings
How settings are asked for and kept
done
Every setting must be set before work starts; none falls back to an assumed default.
At session start the plugin asks in the chat and suggests the worked-out value, used only once you confirm it.
A value set through /plugin configure is accepted too.
Until settings are set every tool is refused except the plugin's own settings script.
Cloud sessions read environment variables first, then the settings file.
Round 2, question 13, what defaults the other settings carry: none; every setting blocks until set.
Round 3, question 1, how a new install asks for settings: in the chat at session start, suggesting the worked-out value.
Round 3, question 2, what waits until settings are set: everything.
Round 4, question 1, how your answer is saved while tools are refused: one allowed command, the settings script.
Round 4, question 2, where cloud sessions keep settings: environment variables set once in the cloud environment.
file
Docs
Documentation and the archivist
done
The archivist moves a long code comment into the docs when the turn ends and leaves a doc-ref pointer.
On someone else's branch it opens an issue instead of moving the comment.
In a repo you don't own, the six-tier docs stay on your machine and out of git unless the owner asks.
Round 1, question 14, whether a long comment moves to the docs automatically: yes, at turn end.
Round 2, question 9, a long comment on someone else's branch: the archivist opens an issue instead.
Round 2, question 10, docs in a repo you don't own: they stay local unless the owner asks.
search
Definitions
What counts as a wholesale rewrite
done
Replacing more than half of a file's lines in one change, or writing the whole file over, is a wholesale rewrite.
It needs your approval by name.
Round 2, question 11, what counts as a wholesale rewrite: over half a file's lines in one change, or the whole file written over.
swap
Fixes
The sixteen mechanical fixes
done
The sixteen fixes listed on docs/plans/2026-10-18-grilling-round-1.html are accepted as listed.
Round 1, question 17, sixteen fixes where one side is plainly out of date: all accepted.
